section_summary: This section documents a 1936 controversy over an Institute of Pacific Relations textbook on Japan prepared for Hawaiian schools and proposed for wider American use. Correspondence among State Department officials, the Institute, and the California Joint Immigration Committee addresses allegations of Japanese propaganda, while confidential State Department memoranda recommend factual corrections concerning the Stimson Doctrine and recognition of Manchukuo. The section concludes with the opening pages of Helen Pratt’s revised experimental textbook, including its preface and discussions of Japanese geography, expansion, society, and Chinese influence.

subfiles.title: Letter from Edward C. Carter to Maxwell M. Hamilton concerning the Hawaii textbook
subfiles.about: Carter thanks Hamilton for returning a mimeographed textbook on Japan and calls attention to a published rebuttal of McClatchy’s criticism.
subfiles.summary: Carter acknowledges the returned textbook from the Institute's Hawaiian office and notes Oscar Shepard answered McClatchy in the New York Times.

subfiles.title: Letter from Maxwell M. Hamilton to Edward C. Carter proposing consultations with the Interior Department
subfiles.about: Hamilton proposes that the Institute send a representative to Washington to discuss Pacific-area textbooks for Hawaii’s public schools.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton refers to earlier conversations with Carter about textbooks on Pacific countries. He reports that Ernest Gruening favors a meeting and offers to connect an Institute representative with the appropriate Department of the Interior official.

subfiles.title: Letter from V. S. McClatchy to Stanley K. Hornbeck transmitting material on school propaganda
subfiles.about: McClatchy forwards a statement about alleged propaganda in public schools and its relationship to Hawaiian statehood.
subfiles.summary: McClatchy calls school propaganda a matter of vital national interest and encloses material prepared for the Commonwealth Club of California.

subfiles.title: Text Books and Courses for Use in Public Schools on Pacific Relations and the History and Culture of Asiatic Peoples
subfiles.about: This title sheet introduces a compilation about Pacific-relations curricula in Hawaii and the continental United States.
subfiles.summary: Cover sheet for a compilation on textbooks and courses on Pacific relations and Asian peoples, affecting Hawaii and the mainland.

subfiles.title: Letter to Walter F. Lafrenz on Institute of Pacific Relations textbook plans
subfiles.from: V. S. McClatchy, California Joint Immigration Committee
subfiles.about: McClatchy supplies documents alleging Japanese participation in plans for Pacific-relations and Japanese-culture courses in American schools.
subfiles.summary: Letter to Lafrenz responding to an Institute of Pacific Relations presentation, alleging coordination with Japan's Society of International Cultural Relations and citing the Hawaiian textbook.

subfiles.title: Letter from V. S. McClatchy to Riley H. Allen concerning the Hawaiian Japan textbook
subfiles.about: McClatchy argues that a Hawaiian textbook on Japan misrepresents historical facts and should not be used in Hawaii or introduced elsewhere.
subfiles.summary: McClatchy tells Riley Allen that textbooks must be free of foreign propaganda and that neither the sponsors nor the authors should control a revision of the Hawaiian Japan textbook.

subfiles.title: Letter from W. K. Lyman to George M. Collins alleging Japanese educational propaganda plans
subfiles.about: Lyman warns Honolulu’s school commissioners about reported Japanese government plans to distribute national-defense and cultural materials in Hawaiian schools.
subfiles.summary: Lyman describes alleged Japanese conference-approved projects for Japanese-language school materials and free references for Hawaiian public schools, quoting Okada and Aoki; he argues this undermines Americanization.

subfiles.title: Hawaiian Troubles Come to Mainland: Propaganda in Public Schools
subfiles.about: The release alleges that a Hawaiian textbook on Japan distorts Japanese immigration and expansionist history and may influence California curricula.
subfiles.summary: Press release: a copy of the textbook and objections went to California school superintendent Kersey; the committee says it minimizes or misrepresents events in Manchuria, Shanghai, Korea and the Gentlemen's Agreement.

subfiles.title: High School Students in U.S. to Be Given Books with Correct Information on Japan
subfiles.from: Japan Times and Mail, reprinted by the California Joint Immigration Committee
subfiles.about: The item reports a Japanese-American plan to compile high-school teaching material about modern Japan for use in the United States.
subfiles.summary: Reprinted item: the Society of International Cultural Relations plans to compile material for Lasker's review and joint American-Japanese revision into books on modern Japan.

subfiles.title: Japan Invades the Public Schools: What Hawaiian Students Are Taught
subfiles.about: The release attacks a Hawaiian textbook’s treatment of Japanese expansion and immigration to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Press release: Japan Invades the Public Schools alleges the textbook understates Japanese actions in Manchuria, Shanghai and Korea and disputes its account of the Gentlemen's Agreement and the 1924 Act.

subfiles.title: Letter acknowledging McClatchy’s materials on public-school propaganda
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges and comments favorably on the importance of McClatchy’s submission concerning school propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks McClatchy for papers on proposed courses on Pacific relations and Japanese culture and agrees school propaganda is of vital national interest.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Japan Invades the Public Schools
subfiles.about: This duplicate release criticizes a Hawaiian textbook’s accounts of Japanese expansion and immigration.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate of Japan Invades the Public Schools, repeating allegations on Manchuria, Shanghai, Korea and the 1924 exclusion law as replacement for the failed agreement.

subfiles.title: Letter from Frederick V. Field sending the revised experimental textbook
subfiles.about: Field sends Hornbeck the revised experimental edition of the Institute’s Japan textbook and requests suggestions.
subfiles.summary: Field says a revised experimental textbook for Hawaii's high schools is being sent separately and invites Hornbeck's suggestions.

subfiles.title: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs divider
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: This departmental sheet separates the correspondence concerning the revised Japan textbook.
subfiles.summary: Divider bearing the name of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs.

subfiles.title: Letter acknowledging receipt of Japan—Where Ancient Loyalties Survive
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges receipt of Helen Pratt’s revised textbook and promises further comment after reviewing it.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck acknowledges Helen Pratt's Japan—Where Ancient Loyalties Survive, accepts Field's invitation to suggest improvements, and will respond after examining it.

subfiles.title: Strictly confidential letter transmitting factual comments on Helen Pratt’s textbook
subfiles.about: Hornbeck confidentially transmits State Department suggestions for correcting factual statements in Helen Pratt’s textbook.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck reports that the Department found much valuable and interesting material in the work. He encloses factual suggestions without accepting departmental responsibility for either the comments or unaddressed portions of the text. Field is asked to treat both the letter and memorandum as strictly confidential.

subfiles.title: Memorandum commenting on the Stimson Doctrine and recognition of Manchukuo
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum recommends more precise language about British policy in World War I, the Stimson Doctrine, and nonrecognition of Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum on the textbook: questions the claim Britain discouraged Japan in World War I, explains the 1932 Stimson notes invoked the Pact of Paris beyond the Open Door, and cautions on how Manchukuo's recognition is described.

subfiles.title: Draft confidential letter transmitting textbook comments
subfiles.about: This draft version of the confidential covering letter transmits a memorandum of factual suggestions on Pratt’s textbook.
subfiles.summary: Draft confidential letter transmitting comments, repeating a favorable general assessment while disclaiming responsibility for suggestions; revisions refine the disclaimer.

subfiles.title: Working and replacement pages for the memorandum on the Stimson Doctrine and Manchukuo
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: These alternate pages revise the memorandum’s explanation of the Stimson Doctrine and the grounds for withholding recognition from Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Working and replacement pages for the Stimson Doctrine memorandum, distinguishing the 1915 Open Door from 1932 nonrecognition via the Pact of Paris and recommending expanded textbook language.

subfiles.title: Japan—Where Ancient Loyalties Survive, experimental edition, opening pages
subfiles.from: Helen Pratt and the American Council, Institute of Pacific Relations
subfiles.about: The opening of the revised experimental textbook introduces Japan through its social contradictions, geography, imperial position, and early adoption of Chinese culture.
subfiles.summary: The excerpt contains duplicate title pages, the Peoples of the Pacific series list, contents, and a preface acknowledging numerous scholarly advisers and source permissions. An introductory section contrasts traditional and Westernized aspects of Japanese life, while Chapter 1 discusses the islands’ geography, natural disasters, mythology, colonial expansion, strategic position, and arguments about Japan’s world mission. Chapter 2 begins an account of persistent clan and imperial traditions and of Japan’s adoption and modification of Chinese governmental, religious, artistic, and writing systems. The text reaches the establishment of Nara and the economic and political weaknesses of the Taika-era reforms before continuing beyond this section.
